reading.body:
Nonprofit AI adoption is measured by sector research organizations, not a real-time registry, and the binding constraint is governance capacity rather than compute or power.

The seven sources split the problem into distinct angles. CEP and NTEN survey how foundations and nonprofits use AI for operations, program delivery, and communications. The AI Equity Project tracks access and training gaps. Candid tracks grantmaking for AI adoption and technology infrastructure. Census BTOS includes nonprofit-heavy service sectors in its adoption series, and Stanford HAI reports macro social impact. No single entity maintains a real-time registry.

The practical uses named are grant writing, donor analytics, and service delivery on small budgets. Because governance capacity is the stated constraint, AI scaling in this sector is limited by oversight and policy adoption, not by access to compute or grid power. The data does not support a compute or power constraint for nonprofits.

The data does not provide adoption rates, budget figures, or compute and power requirements. It identifies who publishes sector research, not how many nonprofits have deployed AI or what infrastructure they use.

summary: Grant writing, donor analytics, and service delivery are the practical uses; governance capacity is the constraint. No single entity keeps a real-time registry of nonprofit AI adoption - coverage comes from sector research organizations, and this page names the ones that actually publish it.

analysis.body:
The closest official measurement for this sector comes from the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, which asks firms whether they used AI in the last two weeks. For Other services, the NAICS 81 grouping that includes grantmaking and civic organizations, 15.0% answered yes in the latest period, against 13.7% in the prior period. The question was first asked in September 2023. That figure covers a broader service category than nonprofits alone, so it should be read as the nearest available proxy rather than a nonprofit-specific count.

On what the technology is actually used for, Candid describes a shift on the funding side, noting that donors are increasingly using AI tools to research causes and charities, which means many won't ever see a nonprofit's website, donation page, or newsletter. The Center for Effective Philanthropy examines how foundations and nonprofits use AI for operations, program delivery, and communications. NTEN runs regular sector-wide research on technology investment, digital maturity, and AI policy adoption among nonprofits. The practical territory these sources describe is grant writing, donor analytics, and service delivery carried out on small budgets, with governance capacity as the binding constraint.

Where money and organizations concentrate is only partly visible in this material. Candid tracks grantmaking trends, including funding directed toward AI adoption and technology infrastructure. The World of AI's own catalogue of nonprofits and open source foundations lists four individually verified organizations, each with a sourced classification note. LMSYS is the most directly AI-central, stewarding Chatbot Arena, a shared evaluation platform used to benchmark model quality. Khan Academy is an end-user of AI capability in education rather than a producer of it, and the Krita Foundation and Blender Foundation steward creative software that AI-generated imagery and 3D content increasingly intersect with. The catalogue states plainly what it does not cover: no training compute providers, no standards bodies setting grid or data-center specifications, and no open-model foundations releasing weights. Its notes confirm organizational structure and nonprofit status, not funding scale, compute access, or governance detail.

The access gap gets separate treatment. The AI Equity Project builds structured learning pathways and intergenerational programs, and transforms public libraries and community spaces into interactive learning environments that bring senior citizens and student volunteers together around practical AI tools. It operates as a global network providing standardized technical curricula and training assets to underrepresented communities, and runs the International AI for Impact Challenge, where top participants secure engineering lab partnerships, academic research access, and intellectual property advisement. NTEN frames the same problem as a structural one, stating that nonprofit technology is marked by inequities within organizations and across the sector that must be dismantled, and it asks practitioners to pledge to use its Equity Guide in their work.

For the broader trajectory, Stanford HAI's AI Index reports a widening gap between what AI can do and how prepared institutions are to manage it, with technical capabilities improving, investment accelerating, and adoption spreading while the frameworks needed to govern, evaluate, and understand the technology fall behind. The Index also notes that data transparency is declining and argues that independent, rigorous measurement matters more in that environment. Stanford HAI itself relies on philanthropic support for the program, which is a reminder that the sector's own funding model shapes what gets measured.

A reader deciding whether to deploy should take from this that the measured adoption base is modest and the constraint named across these sources is governance capacity rather than tool availability, particularly for organizations operating on small budgets. The sources here report no return-on-investment figures for nonprofit AI deployments, and the catalogue of AI-focused nonprofits explicitly declines to speak to funding scale or compute access, so claims about payoff in this sector are not supported by the material gathered here. What is supported is a donor-facing shift that changes how causes get found, a set of operational uses in grant writing, donor analytics, and service delivery, and an equity and training gap that the sector's own technology organizations treat as unresolved.

https://cep.org/.brief: The page from the Center for Effective Philanthropy features an article by Kevin Bolduc, who is identified as vice president of assessment and advisory services. The article’s title asks how one collaborative’s movement-led participatory model makes a difference for grantees. The harvested text does not include any further details or findings.

https://candid.org/.brief: Candid says it provides comprehensive grants and nonprofit data to help users find funding, research nonprofits, and connect with funders. The page also notes that donors are increasingly using AI tools to research causes and charities. According to the text, this means many donors will never see a nonprofit's website, donation page, or newsletter.

https://www.nten.org/.brief: NTEN presents itself as a nonprofit community focused on using technology for social change. It offers networking opportunities, job listings, and professional development resources such as certificates and scholarships. Members can pledge to use an Equity Guide and support open-source developers. NTEN also encourages participation in committees on accessibility, equity, and programs.

https://theaiequityproject.org/.brief: The AI Equity Project reports that it develops structured educational routes and cross-generational initiatives aimed at making AI usable, ethical, and practical for every community. It says it converts public libraries and local community venues into hands-on learning settings where older adults and student volunteers jointly try out practical AI tools. The organization also describes a worldwide network that supplies standardized technical curricula and training materials to underrepresented groups, with support structures meant to ensure each student directly helps deploy machine learning architectures. Its International AI for Impact Challenge asks engineering candidates to propose operational algorithms for real-world issues, and top entrants receive engineering lab partnerships, academic research access, and intellectual property advice.

https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index.brief: The AI Index, an independent initiative at Stanford HAI led by an interdisciplinary steering committee, describes its mission as supplying unbiased, rigorously vetted and globally sourced data on AI to policymakers, researchers, journalists, executives and the public. The current edition reports a widening gap between what AI can do and how prepared institutions are to manage it, saying that technical capabilities, investment and adoption are advancing while the frameworks to govern, evaluate and understand the technology lag, and that data transparency in the field is declining. The page states that previous editions have been cited in The New York Times, Bloomberg and The Guardian, drawn hundreds of academic citations, and been referenced by policymakers in the United States, the United Kingdom and the European Union. It also describes a collaboration with Dr. Elif Kiesow Cortez, founder and leader of the AI & LegTech Lab at The Hague University of Applied Sciences, on a project using a judicial decision database to improve predictability and legal certainty for providers and users of AI technology. The page identifies the 2024 report as the seventh edition.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/ec.brief: The World of AI's catalogue lists four individually verified organisations in this category ,  two nonprofits and two open-source foundations ,  each carrying a classification note sourced to a document the organisation published about itself, with the source and the date it was last read recorded. The page describes LMSYS as the most directly AI-central entry, stewarding Chatbot Arena, a shared evaluation platform the wider AI community uses to benchmark model quality, and notes that such neutral evaluation sits outside the commercial incentives of the labs being assessed. Khan Academy is characterised as an end-user of AI capability in education rather than a producer, while the Krita Foundation and Blender Foundation steward creative software that AI-generated imagery and 3D content increasingly intersect with, though their missions predate AI. The page states that none of the four are infrastructure builders in the compute-or-power sense, and that it covers no training compute providers, no standards bodies setting grid or data-centre specifications, and no open-model foundations releasing weights. It adds that the notes confirm only organisational structure and nonprofit status, not funding scale, compute access or governance detail.
